## 1. Purpose

This SOP describes standardized procedures for recording geographic
coordinates, navigating to field sites, and managing waypoint data.
Accurate and consistent location data are essential for linking field
observations to spatial analyses, returning to the same sampling points
across seasons, and sharing site information among researchers. This
SOP covers handheld GPS receivers, smartphone GPS applications, and
post-field data management.


## 2. Scope

- **Applies to:** All EA Program field activities that require
  geographic coordinates, including sample collection, transect
  establishment, monitoring well location, equipment installation, and
  site reconnaissance
- **Does not apply to:** High-precision survey-grade GNSS work
  (sub-centimeter accuracy); drone-based georeferencing (see
  [SOP-F630](SOP-F630-drone-operations.qmd)); GIS post-processing and
  spatial analysis (see future SOP-L804)
- **Location:** All EA Program field sites


## 3. Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                                          |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| PI / Field Lead   | Approve coordinate system and datum for each project    |
| Trained Personnel | Record waypoints per this SOP, upload data after fieldwork |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent use                |


## 4. Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Physical:** Navigating to remote waypoints may involve uneven
  terrain, dense vegetation, or stream crossings. Do not fixate on
  the GPS screen while walking.
- **Environmental:** Reliance on GPS in areas with poor satellite
  coverage (dense canopy, steep canyons) can lead to navigation
  errors. Always carry a paper map or site sketch as a backup.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Closed-toed shoes or field boots
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)

### Emergency Procedures

Refer to [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd). If lost or
disoriented, stop moving, note your last known coordinates, and contact
the field lead by phone or walkie-talkie.


## 5. Equipment and Materials

| Item                                  | Notes                                    |
|:--------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Handheld GPS receiver (Garmin or equivalent) | Check battery level before departure; carry spare batteries |
| Smartphone with GPS app              | Avenza Maps, Gaia GPS, or similar app with offline map capability |
| Backup paper map or site sketch       | Annotated with known landmarks and access roads |
| Field notebook                        | For recording waypoint IDs and descriptions |
| USB cable or Bluetooth adapter        | For downloading waypoints to a computer  |
| Spare batteries (AA or rechargeable)  | Matched to the GPS unit model            |


## 6. Procedure

### 6.1 Pre-Field Setup

1. Confirm the coordinate system and datum for the project. The EA
   Program default is **WGS 84, latitude/longitude in decimal
   degrees**. If a project requires UTM or NAD 83, configure the
   device accordingly and note the setting in the field notebook.
2. On a handheld GPS, verify the datum setting: navigate to
   Setup > Position Format and confirm WGS 84.
3. On a smartphone app, enable offline maps for the study area. Do
   not rely on cellular data for map tiles in the field.
4. Clear or archive old waypoints from the device so that the day's
   data are easy to identify.
5. Pre-load target waypoints if revisiting known sites. Use the naming
   convention described in Section 6.3.

### 6.2 Recording Waypoints in the Field

1. At the sampling location, hold the GPS receiver at chest height
   in an open area away from dense canopy, cliff faces, and vehicles.
2. Wait until the GPS reports an accuracy of 5 m or better. If
   accuracy remains above 5 m after two minutes, record the waypoint
   and note the reported accuracy in the field notebook.
3. Save the waypoint using the naming convention in Section 6.3.
4. In the field notebook, record:
   - Waypoint name
   - Date and time
   - Coordinates (as displayed on the device)
   - Reported accuracy (HDOP or meters, as available)
   - A brief description (e.g., "upstream riffle, transect 3 start")
5. If using a smartphone, take a screenshot of the GPS display as a
   backup record.

### 6.3 Waypoint Naming Convention

Use the following format for waypoint names:

`SITE_TYPE_NN`

where:

- `SITE` = three- or four-letter site abbreviation (e.g., BFS, THW,
  MRW)
- `TYPE` = two-letter code for the point type (see table below)
- `NN` = sequential two-digit number

| Code | Point Type                | Example     |
|:-----|:--------------------------|:------------|
| WQ   | Water quality sampling    | BFS_WQ_01   |
| SO   | Soil sampling             | THW_SO_03   |
| TR   | Transect endpoint         | MRW_TR_01   |
| WL   | Monitoring well           | BFS_WL_02   |
| RF   | Reference / benchmark     | THW_RF_01   |
| GN   | General / other           | MRW_GN_05   |

If a project requires a different convention, document it in the
project README and field notebook.

### 6.4 Navigating to Existing Waypoints

1. Load the target waypoint on the GPS receiver or smartphone app.
2. Use the "Navigate" or "Go To" function. Follow the bearing
   indicator, checking your surroundings periodically.
3. When the GPS indicates you are within the reported accuracy of the
   waypoint, look for physical markers (flagging, rebar, painted
   rocks) to confirm the exact location.
4. If the physical marker cannot be found, record a new waypoint at
   the location you judge to be correct and note the discrepancy in
   the field notebook.

### 6.5 Post-Field Data Management

1. Download waypoints from the GPS receiver to the project computer
   within 48 hours of returning from the field.
2. Export waypoints as a `.gpx` or `.csv` file and save to the
   project GitHub repository under `data/gps/`.
3. Use the file naming convention:
   `YYYY-MM-DD_SiteID_waypoints.gpx`
4. Verify that waypoint names match the field notebook entries.
   Correct any discrepancies before committing the file.
5. Back up the raw GPS file to the lab shared drive.


## 7. Quality Control

- Compare GPS coordinates against known benchmarks or previously
  recorded waypoints when revisiting sites. Discrepancies greater
  than 10 m should be investigated and noted.
- At least once per semester, verify the GPS receiver against a
  known benchmark (e.g., a USGS survey marker or a campus reference
  point) to confirm the device is functioning properly.
- Record the GPS model, serial number, and firmware version in the
  field notebook at the start of each project.


## 8. References

- Garmin International. *GPSMAP 66 Series Owner's Manual*.
- Avenza Systems. *Avenza Maps User Guide*.

## 10. Training Record

Before using GPS equipment independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Demonstrate proper waypoint recording (datum check, accuracy
   verification, naming convention) during a supervised field visit
3. Successfully download and export waypoints to the project
   repository
4. Be signed off by the PI or field lead
